analysis.one_liner: Taxes carbon in coal, oil, and gas and pays the money back through tax cuts and quarterly rebates.
analysis.headline: A Democratic bill to tax carbon emissions and rebate the money to households drew no cosponsors, went to five committees, and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a fee on the carbon dioxide content of coal, oil, and natural gas, starting at $25 per ton in 2021 and rising $10 each year until emissions targets are met. Producers, miners, and importers would pay the fee. The revenue would go into a Carbon Trust Fund used to cut income tax rates for individuals, pay quarterly cash rebates to people with valid Social Security numbers, and fund help for coal workers and energy and infrastructure projects. A border fee on carbon-heavy imports would keep foreign goods from dodging the tax. The bill was referred to five House committees and died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households would gain twice: individual income tax rates would drop (the 10% rate falls to 9%, the 12% to 11%, the 22% to 21%, and the 24% to 23.5%), and any remaining fund money would be paid out as equal quarterly cash rebates to every eligible adult. Coal workers and coal communities would get transition assistance, and rural energy, grid, and research programs would receive funding. Cleaner energy industries would gain as fossil fuels become more expensive.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households getting rebates and tax cuts

how_it_helps.text: Every person lawfully present with a valid Social Security number would receive an equal quarterly cash rebate from the carbon tax revenue, after income tax cuts and transition programs are funded.
Individual income tax rates would be cut across the four lowest brackets starting in 2022, funded directly by the carbon tax.
Coal workers and coal communities would receive dedicated transition assistance, and 20% of the fund would go to rural energy aid, research, grid improvements, and climate-resilient infrastructure.
A carbon equivalency fee on imports of goods made with fossil fuels would prevent U.S. manufacturers from being undercut by foreign producers that face no carbon price.
The tax would drop to zero for five-year stretches whenever the EPA certifies that emissions-reduction benchmarks — 30% below 2005 levels by 2025, rising to 80% by 2050 — are on track to be met.

analysis.who_pays: Producers, miners, and importers of coal, oil, and natural gas would pay the tax, and some of that cost would reach consumers through higher gasoline, heating, and electricity prices. Households would get the money back through rebates and lower tax rates, but people who cannot claim the rebate — those without a valid Social Security number who are not lawfully present — would bear the higher prices without reimbursement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: Energy prices would rise for everyone beginning in 2022, before any rebate arrives, and households with high fuel use — long commutes, heating-oil homes — could pay more than they get back at first.
The rebates are limited to people with valid Social Security numbers who are lawfully present, so some residents facing the same higher energy prices would receive nothing back.
The carbon equivalency fee on imports would raise prices for imported goods made with fossil fuels, from manufactured products to fuel-intensive goods, adding costs beyond energy bills.
The tax rate would climb $10 per ton every year — roughly doubling every two years early on — a steep schedule that critics would call too fast for households and energy markets to adjust to.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is built to protect ordinary households: most of the money comes back as direct tax cuts and equal quarterly rebates, which for most lower- and middle-income families would exceed their share of the added energy costs, and coal communities get dedicated help. The real costs fall on fossil fuel producers and on consumers during the transition — higher prices at the pump and on the bill before the first rebate check — and on people excluded from the rebate. The steep annual escalation and the multi-agency reporting scheme would make it difficult to administer, but the core trade is straightforward: higher fossil fuel prices in exchange for cash back to households and mandated emissions cuts.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to five different House committees on the same day, and none of them ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerry McNerney introduced the bill on September 4, 2020, late in the 116th Congress.
No member signed on as a cosponsor.

The Speaker sent it to five committees — Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Science, Space, and Technology, Energy and Commerce, and Transportation and Infrastructure — a referral structure that splits a bill's pieces among committees with no clear path to the floor.
The House referred part of it to the Transportation Subcommittee on Highways and Transit on September 8, 2020, and the action history records no hearing, markup, or vote in any committee afterward.
The bill never received a floor vote and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and importers avoided a carbon tax that would have cost them directly, and no member of Congress had to take a recorded vote on energy prices. Households gained nothing, since the rebates and tax cuts were never enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers; households gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Jerry McNerney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the carbon tax and rebate bill and referred it to five committees for consideration.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral; its chair never scheduled a markup
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without any hearing, markup, or vote after it was referred on September 4, 2020.

against.name: Four other committees of referral (Energy and Commerce; Science, Space, and Technology; Education and Labor; Transportation and Infrastructure)
against.role: Committees holding portions of the bill
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup is recorded for any of them.

against.name: Members of the House (0 cosponsors)
against.role: Potential cosponsors who did not sign on
against.what_they_did: No member besides the sponsor signed on to the bill, leaving it with no visible floor support.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no member besides the Democratic sponsor signed on, so the partisan split never got a chance to show itself; the lone supporter was a Democrat.

industries.note: Coal would pay the highest carbon tax per unit of energy of any fossil fuel, cutting demand for it. The bill's own worker-transition fund acknowledges the industry and its communities would shrink.

industries.industry: Oil and natural gas producers and importers
industries.note: Producers, miners, and importers would pay $25 per ton of CO2 starting in 2022, rising $10 annually, with costs passed to consumers at the pump and on energy bills.
As fossil fuels get more expensive, cleaner alternatives become comparatively cheaper, and the bill funds energy research, efficiency, and grid improvements directly.
A carbon equivalency fee would tax imported goods made with fossil fuels, protecting domestic manufacturers but raising prices on those imports for consumers.
